note: All data, names and figures are FICTIONAL. Not real market data, not investment advice.

voices.hanh: Ms. Hanh, the boss: direct, brisk, fair.
voices.khoi: Khoi, the colleague: jokey, a little dramatic, always on your side.
voices.linh: Dr. Linh, the mentor: calm, patient, explains the why.

praise.text: Copies removed, real orders retained. These totals can go to the board.
The export brought twins; you checked their IDs before counting them.
Checking record keys kept duplicate exports from inflating the totals.

miss.text: Copied rows inflated the order total. Reconcile the keys before sending it.
The export got a second helping of the same orders. Let's count each once.
Compare record keys before aggregation to distinguish copies from real repeats.

wrong_fix.text: The fix also removed genuine repeat orders. Restore them and deduplicate by key.
Some regular customers vanished with the copies. Their second orders still count.
A repeated customer is not necessarily a duplicate transaction; check the order key.

praise.text: You separated outage zeros from sales. The demand estimate is better supported.
The shop did not sell zero just because the recorder took a nap. Good catch.
Treating outage zeros as missing preserves the distinction between no sales and no observation.

miss.text: Outage zeros pulled the sales estimate down. Check the recording status.
Our recorder went quiet, and the chart called it a sales drought. Check the outage log.
An outage tells us the value is unknown, not that sales were zero.

wrong_fix.text: The replacement average is unsupported. Mark the gaps and disclose them.
We gave the missing sales imaginary friends. Let's keep the gaps visible instead.
An invented average adds assumptions; retain missing values unless a justified method is stated.

praise.text: Prices now share a unit and currency. We can compare supplier costs.
The prices finally speak the same currency. My calculator can stop translating.
Convert units and currencies consistently before comparing or summing values.

miss.text: The total combines incompatible units. Standardize them before using it.
We added crates to coins and got a very confident mystery number.
Numbers in different units cannot be added meaningfully without conversion.

wrong_fix.text: Some rows still use the old unit. Complete the conversion before reporting.
Half the prices crossed the currency bridge; the others are still waiting.
Apply the conversion rule to every affected row and verify the resulting units.

praise.text: Dates and time zones now align. The daily comparison is usable.
Everyone's clock has joined the same meeting. The daily totals make sense now.
Parsing dates and aligning time zones places observations in comparable daily windows.

miss.text: The daily totals mix date formats and clocks. Normalize both first.
Our Tuesday borrowed a few hours from Wednesday. Let's put them back.
Different date formats or time zones can assign the same event to different days.

wrong_fix.text: The fix assumes identical clocks. Check each source's time zone.
We set every clock by the office kettle. The export needs its own time-zone rules.
Parse each source's date convention and time zone before assigning calendar days.

praise.text: Spelling variants are merged without losing real regions. Use this grouping.
The same region stopped wearing five name badges. Nicely sorted.
Standardizing equivalent labels prevents one category from being split across groups.

miss.text: Typos split the regions and distorted their ranking. Normalize the labels.
One region entered the league three times under different spellings.
Group equivalent spellings together before comparing category totals.

wrong_fix.text: Distinct places were merged. Restore them and use a verified label map.
Two different towns now share a name badge. Let's untangle the guest list.
A spelling resemblance is insufficient; confirm that labels refer to the same category.

praise.text: The entry typo is corrected and the real price move remains. Good judgment.
You removed the extra zero without evicting the actual price jump.
Checking the source lets us correct entry errors while retaining genuine extremes.

miss.text: One entry error dominates the chart. Check it against the source.
That extra zero has taken over the whole meeting. Can we check its paperwork?
Investigate an extreme value before deciding whether it is an error or a real observation.

wrong_fix.text: The fix removed a genuine price move too. Restore it and correct only the typo.
The typo left, but it took a real price jump along for the ride.
An unusual value may be valid; remove or correct it only with supporting evidence.

praise.text: The year-on-year comparison controls for the season. Use that in the forecast.
You checked last year's holiday rush before ordering more shelves. Sensible.
Comparing equivalent seasonal periods helps separate recurring patterns from trend.

miss.text: The forecast treats a seasonal peak as lasting growth. Compare like periods.
The calendar did its usual dance, and we called it a growth strategy.
A recurring seasonal rise is not evidence of a sustained trend on its own.

wrong_fix.text: A straight line misses the seasonal cycle. Use comparable periods.
We put a ruler on a wave. It still comes back next season.
A linear fit alone does not account for a repeating seasonal pattern.

praise.text: Group results and their weights are clear. The overall winner needs that context.
The grand total tried to steal the show; you gave the groups their lines back.
Examining group rates and group sizes can explain why an aggregate comparison reverses.

miss.text: The aggregate hides the group results. Show both before choosing a winner.
The headline total won the debate before the groups even got a chair.
A change in group composition can reverse the pattern seen within each group.

wrong_fix.text: The split is useful, but the weights are missing. Include group sizes.
We invited the groups but forgot to count how many people each brought.
Within-group rates need their denominators to explain the aggregate result.

praise.text: You flagged the small sample. Keep the forecast cautious.
Five observations did not get promoted to universal law today. Good call.
A small sample carries substantial uncertainty, so its conclusion needs qualification.

miss.text: The claim is too strong for this sample. State the count and uncertainty.
A handful of cases is doing a stadium-sized impression. Let's turn down the volume.
With few observations, random variation can look like a strong pattern.

wrong_fix.text: The small group disappeared from the report. Restore it with a caveat.
The tiny group needs a warning label, not a trapdoor.
Report the small group's result and sample size rather than hiding it.

praise.text: The report says associated, with no unsupported causal claim. Approved.
The two lines moved together; you resisted giving one the steering wheel.
Association alone cannot establish causation; other factors may influence both variables.

miss.text: The causal claim exceeds the evidence. Check alternative explanations.
Those lines are travel companions; we have not proved which one drives.
Observational association can reflect confounding, reverse causation, or chance.

wrong_fix.text: The revision denies the association too. Keep the observed link, qualify the cause.
We took away the steering wheel and accidentally erased the road.
Rejecting a causal interpretation does not erase an observed association.

praise.text: The report includes false alarms and prevalence. That supports the risk estimate.
You counted the false alarms as well as the sirens. My ears thank you.
The chance a flag is correct depends on prevalence as well as the test's error rates.

miss.text: A flag is presented as near certainty. Include the underlying event rate.
Our alarm shouts loudly, but rare events still need a head count.
When an event is rare, false positives may outnumber true positives even with a useful test.

wrong_fix.text: Discarding the alarm loses useful information. Recalculate using the base rate.
The alarm needs context, not early retirement.
Combine prevalence and error rates to interpret the signal rather than rejecting it entirely.

praise.text: You checked which accounts were excluded. The risk claim now has context.
You asked about the shops missing from the reunion photo. That matters.
An analysis of survivors alone may omit failures and misrepresent the original population.

miss.text: The estimate only includes surviving accounts. Identify the missing group.
Our reunion photo makes everyone look successful; the absent shops need a mention.
Selection into the observed sample can bias conclusions about the full population.

wrong_fix.text: Missing does not mean failed. Verify those accounts before classifying them.
An empty chair is not a bankruptcy certificate. Let's check who is missing.
Determine why observations are absent rather than assuming a single outcome for them.

praise.text: The full period is shown. We can judge the campaign in context.
You opened the whole album instead of just the flattering photo.
A consistent, justified time window reduces the risk of selecting only favorable results.

miss.text: The selected window overstates performance. Show the full relevant period.
That chart picked its best week for the office portrait. Let's see the rest.
Changing the time window can change the story; inspect the broader period before concluding.

wrong_fix.text: Show the broader evidence rather than assigning motives.
The chart needs more dates, not a courtroom scene.
Explain how the full period changes the result without inferring someone's intent.

praise.text: The bars start at zero and show units. The size difference is clear.
The bars have their feet on the same floor again. Much less dramatic.
A zero baseline lets bar lengths represent quantities proportionally.

miss.text: The cut-off axis magnifies the gap. Reset the baseline and label units.
Those bars are standing on a hidden box. Let's put them back on the floor.
Truncating a bar chart's baseline can exaggerate a small difference.

wrong_fix.text: Changing chart type left the axis issue unresolved. Fix the scale.
The chart changed clothes but kept the same platform shoes.
Check the baseline and units directly; a different chart type alone does not fix them.

praise.text: Unique customers are counted across both lists. Use that total.
Customers can visit twice without becoming two people. You kept the head count honest.
Deduplicating overlapping customer sets gives the size of their union.

miss.text: The lists overlap, so their sum overstates customers. Match the identifiers.
Some customers got two seats in our head count. Let's check the overlap.
Adding list sizes double-counts customers present in more than one list.

wrong_fix.text: Dropping a whole list loses valid customers. Reconcile the overlap instead.
We solved the seating problem by closing half the room. Let's reopen it.
Retain customers unique to either list while counting shared identifiers once.

praise.text: The unfinished day is excluded and disclosed. The comparison is fair.
Today's export had not finished breakfast. You gave it time before judging sales.
Compare complete periods and state when incomplete observations are excluded.

miss.text: The apparent crash comes from incomplete data. Check arrival status.
The numbers are still on the delivery truck, but the chart has declared a crisis.
A partial final day can resemble a decline even when the underlying activity is stable.

wrong_fix.text: The exclusion needs a note. Tell readers why the last day is absent.
The last day slipped out the back door; leave readers a note.
Disclose the cutoff so readers understand which complete periods were compared.

praise.text: Effect size and significance are both reported. We can assess the test.
You asked how big the lift was and whether luck could explain it. Two useful questions.
Effect size describes the estimated change; a significance test assesses compatibility with the null.

miss.text: There is no significance check behind this winner. Assess the uncertainty.
The winning variant has a trophy but no uncertainty check. Let's do the paperwork.
A measured difference alone does not establish that the evidence is strong enough to select a winner.

wrong_fix.text: The p-value is not the chance the change works. Correct that explanation.
That p-value is answering a different question from the one on its name badge.
A p-value concerns data under the null model, not the probability that a change succeeds.

praise.text: You waited for the planned sample. The decision follows the test design.
The test got to finish its shift before we crowned a winner.
Following the planned stopping rule avoids the false-positive risk of repeated early checks.

miss.text: The test stopped at a favorable peek. Use the planned stopping rule.
We called the match at the first good score. The test still had time on the clock.
Repeatedly checking and stopping when significance appears can inflate false positives.

wrong_fix.text: Keep the evidence, but explain the early stopping and its limits.
No need to throw the whole test into the shredder; its stopping rule needs a footnote.
An early peek calls for qualified interpretation or a valid sequential method, not automatic deletion.

praise.text: The result is marked inconclusive. That is the right decision for this sample.
No winner today, and the report says so. The trophy can stay in the cupboard.
An underpowered test may miss a meaningful effect, so non-significance is not proof of equality.

miss.text: The test cannot establish no difference. Check its power and sample size.
The test whispered, and we translated it as a firm no. Let's check the sample.
A non-significant result may reflect insufficient data rather than the absence of an effect.

wrong_fix.text: A few hundred users do not settle this test. Revisit the planned sample.
We found a bigger handful, but it still may not fill the sample plan.
Choose sample size from the effect of interest and desired power before declaring a winner.

praise.text: Step conversion rates identify the weakest stage. Focus the repair there.
You found the leaky step instead of blaming the biggest bucket.
Compare adjacent-step conversion rates to locate disproportionate funnel losses.

miss.text: Raw losses alone do not locate the problem. Compare step rates.
The first bucket is biggest, so its spill looks loudest. Check the rates too.
A large raw drop can simply reflect a large starting population; use step denominators.

wrong_fix.text: The partial last day distorts later steps. Compare complete periods.
Some customers are still walking down the funnel. Let's not mark them missing yet.
Incomplete recent periods can bias downstream conversion when events arrive with a delay.

praise.text: Cohorts are compared at the same age. The retention claim is supported.
The new sign-ups cannot hide the leavers in this chart. Nice detective work.
Comparing cohorts at equal ages separates retention from changes in acquisition volume.

miss.text: New arrivals hide existing-customer churn. Show cohort retention.
The welcome party is busy enough to hide the exit queue. Let's check cohorts.
A growing customer total can coexist with poor retention when acquisition offsets churn.

wrong_fix.text: Old and young cohorts need matching ages. Align their observation windows.
We compared a first day with a tenth birthday. Let's line up the calendars.
Compare the same time since joining so each cohort has an equivalent opportunity to return.

praise.text: The report shows both opposing segment moves. That explains the flat total.
The average said nothing happened; the segments brought two different stories.
An aggregate can mask offsetting changes, so inspect relevant segments.

miss.text: The flat average hides opposite movements. Break it down.
Two teams pulled in opposite directions, and the average took a nap.
Examine meaningful subgroups when a stable overall measure may conceal changing composition.

wrong_fix.text: The segments are now too small to interpret. Use fewer, meaningful groups.
We sliced the cake so thin nobody can taste it. Broader groups may help.
Too many small slices increase noise; balance business relevance with adequate sample sizes.

praise.text: The drilldown accounts for the full drop. We have a focused next step.
You followed the crumbs past the first plausible sandwich. The drop finally adds up.
A useful drilldown checks whether the identified segment explains the observed overall change.

miss.text: The first explanation is untested. Quantify which segment accounts for the drop.
The first suspect had a convincing hat. Let's still check the numbers.
Test plausible explanations against segment contributions before naming the source of a decline.

wrong_fix.text: The economy is a hypothesis, not evidence. Show the relevant splits.
The economy got blamed before we opened a single drawer. Let's look inside.
A broad explanation needs supporting comparisons and a quantified link to the observed change.

praise.text: The untreated comparison puts the rebound in context. Keep that caveat.
The worst week bounced back, but you checked whether everyone else bounced too.
Comparable untreated shops help distinguish an intervention from a natural return toward typical levels.

miss.text: The report credits a natural rebound to the fix. Add a comparison group.
We gave the repair a medal for a bounce that might have happened anyway.
Selecting extreme performers can produce a later rebound even without an effective intervention.

wrong_fix.text: The same noise cannot establish that the fix backfired. Check the comparison.
The medal became a complaint form awfully fast. We still need the comparison shops.
A noisy reversal alone supports neither benefit nor harm; use an appropriate untreated comparison.

praise.text: Match rates were checked after the join. The customer totals are traceable.
You checked who made it through the join door. No silent disappearing act.
Auditing matched and unmatched keys reveals records lost during a join.

miss.text: The join dropped customers silently. Inspect unmatched keys before reporting.
The join held a meeting and forgot to invite some customer IDs.
A join can change the population; compare row counts and key coverage before and after.

wrong_fix.text: Names are not unique identifiers. Restore a validated key.
Two customers share a name, and the join thinks they share a wallet.
Use a stable, appropriately unique key and check its cardinality before joining.

praise.text: Test accounts are filtered with a stated rule. These are customer metrics.
The staff's practice clicks no longer count as a customer stampede.
A documented test-account filter separates internal activity from genuine customer behavior.

miss.text: Staff test clicks inflated the customer metric. Apply the account rule.
The office testing party showed up as customer growth. Let's check the guest list.
Internal test activity can bias metrics unless identified and consistently excluded.

wrong_fix.text: Real power users were removed too. Filter by verified test status.
Our busiest customers got mistaken for staff. They deserve their seats back.
High activity alone is not evidence of a test account; use verified identifiers or flags.

praise.text: Subtotal and header rows are excluded. The total now counts detail rows once.
The total stopped adding itself to itself. A small victory for arithmetic.
Exclude summary and repeated header rows before aggregating the underlying records.

miss.text: The sum includes its own subtotals. Separate detail from summary rows.
The totals came back for seconds. Let's serve only the detail rows.
Adding detail and subtotal rows double-counts the same underlying values.

wrong_fix.text: Blank regions can be valid records. Remove rows by their role, not that field alone.
A missing region is not a subtotal disguise. Check the row before showing it out.
Use evidence that a row is a summary or header rather than deleting all incomplete labels.

praise.text: Refunds remain and cancellations are separated. Net revenue is clearer.
Refunds kept their minus signs; cancelled orders left the sales queue.
Refunds reverse revenue, while cancelled orders should not be treated as completed sales.

miss.text: Cancelled orders are counted as revenue. Separate them from completed sales.
Some orders never left the starting line but still got a sales medal.
Use order status to distinguish cancellations from sales and their later refunds.

wrong_fix.text: Removing refunds overstates revenue. Restore those valid negative entries.
The refunds were inconvenient, but the cash still went back. Keep them in the books.
Valid refund amounts belong in net revenue; a negative sign alone does not indicate an error.

praise.text: The cutoff is identified. We will compare only equivalent coverage.
You spotted that the file left work early. No full-year verdict from half a shift.
Check temporal coverage before comparing totals from periods of different lengths.

miss.text: This export ends early. A partial year cannot support the full-year comparison.
The file ran out of pages, and we called it a business slump.
A truncated export can mimic a decline because later observations are absent.

wrong_fix.text: The extrapolation is undisclosed. Show observed coverage and any assumptions.
We filled missing months with invisible pencil. Readers need to see the assumptions.
If extrapolation is justified, label it and explain its uncertainty rather than presenting it as observed data.

praise.text: All identified defects were checked. The final result has an audit trail.
You fixed the whole queue of defects, not just the loudest one.
An ordered audit and validation after each step help handle interacting data defects.

miss.text: One repair left other defects unresolved. Run the remaining checks.
One gremlin left, but its colleagues are still in the spreadsheet.
Fixing a single issue does not validate the rest of a file; continue the audit.

wrong_fix.text: The cleaning removed real variation. Restore valid values and narrow the rules.
The spreadsheet is spotless because we polished away part of the business.
Validate each transformation against source evidence so cleaning preserves genuine variation.

praise.text: Mean and median are both reported. Typical ticket size is clearer.
The giant tickets no longer get to speak for every ticket.
For skewed values, the median complements the mean by describing a less tail-sensitive center.

miss.text: The mean alone is not representative here. Include the median and spread.
A few marathon tickets made every job look like an all-day expedition.
A long tail can pull the mean far from a typical observation; inspect the distribution too.

wrong_fix.text: Long tickets may be valid. Restore them and report the skew.
The marathon tickets are still real work, even if they spoil the average.
Retain valid extremes and use suitable summaries rather than deleting the tail to make a neat average.
